lessons.title: Line, Shape, and Form
lessons.content: Line is the most basic element — a mark moving through space. Lines can be straight, curved, thick, thin. They create direction and emotion: horizontal = calm, vertical = strong, diagonal = dynamic, zigzag = energy. Shapes are 2D: geometric (circles, squares) or organic (irregular). Forms are 3D: spheres, cubes. Artists use shading to make shapes look like forms. Everything starts with basic shapes.
examples: A tree: trunk = rectangle, canopy = organic shape, branches = curved lines
Shading a circle into a sphere: light side, gradual transition, dark, cast shadow
Picasso simplified faces into geometric shapes

keyTerms.line: Most fundamental element — mark moving through space
keyTerms.contour: The outline or edge of a shape or form
keyTerms.gesture line: A quick, flowing line capturing movement and energy

quiz.explanation: Shading creates illusion of form.

quiz.question: Diagonal lines feel:
quiz.explanation: Movement and energy.

quiz.explanation: Light and shadow create depth.

options: Irregular, natural forms like leaves and clouds
quiz.explanation: Found in nature — free-flowing, not geometric.

quiz.question: A gesture line captures:
options: Movement and energy in a quick sketch
quiz.explanation: Fast, flowing lines convey the essence and motion of a subject.

lessons.title: Color Theory
lessons.content: Primary colors (red, blue, yellow) can't be made by mixing. Secondary: red+blue=purple, red+yellow=orange, blue+yellow=green. Tertiary: primary + adjacent secondary. Color wheel organizes all colors. Complementary: opposite on wheel (red-green) — strong contrast. Analogous: adjacent (blue, blue-green, green) — harmony. Properties: hue (name), value (light/dark), saturation (vivid/dull).
examples: Complementary: red flower against green leaves stands out
Sunset: analogous warm colors — red, orange, yellow
Tint: white + red = pink. Shade: black + red = maroon

keyTerms.complementary: Opposite on color wheel — maximum contrast
keyTerms.warm colors: Red, orange, yellow — feel energetic and advancing
keyTerms.cool colors: Blue, green, purple — feel calm and receding

quiz.question: Primary colors:
quiz.explanation: Can't be made by mixing.

quiz.question: Red and green are:
quiz.explanation: Opposite on wheel.

quiz.question: White + color =:
quiz.explanation: White lightens.

quiz.question: Warm colors make objects appear to:
quiz.explanation: Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) advance visually.

quiz.question: Saturation refers to:
options: How vivid or dull a color is
quiz.explanation: High saturation = vivid. Low saturation = muted/gray.

lessons.title: Texture, Space, and Composition
lessons.content: Texture: how surface feels or looks. Actual (touchable) or visual (implied by art). Space: positive (subject) vs negative (empty around it). Perspective creates depth — objects smaller with distance, lines converge at vanishing point. Composition: arrangement of elements. Rule of Thirds: place subject at intersection of 3×3 grid. Balance, contrast, and focal point guide the viewer's eye.
examples: Van Gogh's thick brushstrokes create visual texture
FedEx logo: arrow hidden in negative space
Rule of Thirds: horizon on top or bottom third line

keyTerms.rule of thirds: Placing subjects at grid intersections for dynamic composition
keyTerms.focal point: The area that draws the viewer's eye first

quiz.question: Negative space:
quiz.explanation: Background and surrounding space.

quiz.question: Rule of Thirds:
quiz.explanation: Off-center = more dynamic.

quiz.question: Depth on flat surface:
quiz.explanation: Size, overlap, and converging lines.

quiz.question: A focal point is:
options: The area that draws the viewer's eye first
The center of the canvas always
quiz.explanation: Created through contrast, detail, or isolation — not always in the center.

quiz.question: Visual texture differs from actual texture because:
options: It's an illusion created by the artist — you can't feel it
quiz.explanation: A painting of tree bark looks rough but the canvas surface is smooth.

lessons.title: Principles of Design
lessons.content: The principles of design guide how elements are organized in artwork. Balance: visual weight distributed evenly — symmetrical (mirror image) or asymmetrical (different elements balance each other). Contrast: differences that create visual interest — light vs dark, large vs small, rough vs smooth. Emphasis: making one element stand out as the focal point. Movement: guiding the viewer's eye through the artwork using lines, shapes, and color. Pattern: repeating elements creating rhythm and visual interest. Unity: all elements work together as a cohesive whole — nothing feels out of place. Proportion: the relationship between sizes of different elements. These principles work together — a successful artwork uses several of them in harmony.
examples: Symmetrical balance: a butterfly — mirror image left and right
Contrast: a single red flower in a field of green — emphasis through color contrast
Movement: a winding path in a landscape painting leads the eye from foreground to background

keyTerms.balance: Even distribution of visual weight — symmetrical or asymmetrical
keyTerms.contrast: Differences between elements creating visual interest
keyTerms.emphasis: Making one element dominate as the focal point
keyTerms.unity: All elements working together as a cohesive whole
keyTerms.proportion: The size relationship between different elements in an artwork

quiz.question: Asymmetrical balance means:
options: Different elements balance each other visually without being identical
Everything is the same on both sides
quiz.explanation: A large shape on one side can balance several small shapes on the other.

quiz.question: Emphasis is created by:
options: Making one element stand out through contrast, size, color, or isolation
quiz.explanation: The focal point draws attention — achieved through differences from surrounding elements.

quiz.question: Pattern in art creates:

quiz.explanation: Repeating elements (shapes, colors, lines) create visual rhythm.

quiz.question: Unity means:
options: All elements work together — nothing feels out of place
quiz.explanation: A unified artwork feels complete — every element contributes to the whole.

quiz.question: Proportion affects how we perceive:
options: Scale, importance, and relationships between parts
quiz.explanation: Exaggerated proportions can create emphasis, humor, or emotional impact.

lessons.title: Light and Shadow
lessons.content: Light and shadow are fundamental to creating realistic art and mood. Every 3D object has: a highlight (brightest point where light directly hits), midtone (the object's true color), core shadow (darkest part of the object opposite the light), reflected light (light bouncing from nearby surfaces onto the shadow side), and cast shadow (the shadow the object creates on surrounding surfaces). Value is the range from light to dark — a value scale goes from white to black with many grays between. High contrast (strong darks and lights) creates drama and energy. Low contrast (similar values) creates calm and softness. Chiaroscuro is the dramatic use of light and dark pioneered by artists like Caravaggio and Rembrandt. Understanding how light falls on objects is the key to drawing and painting realistically.
examples: Hold a ball under a desk lamp — observe highlight, midtone, core shadow, reflected light, and cast shadow
Rembrandt lighting: dramatic side light with one side bright and the other in deep shadow — still used in photography
A white egg on white paper: value differences are subtle — training your eye to see them improves all your art

keyTerms.value: The range from light to dark in artwork
keyTerms.highlight: The brightest point where light hits directly
keyTerms.core shadow: The darkest part of an object — opposite the light source
keyTerms.chiaroscuro: Dramatic contrast between light and dark — used for theatrical effect
keyTerms.cast shadow: The shadow an object creates on surrounding surfaces

quiz.question: The core shadow is:
options: The darkest part of the object, opposite the light source
The cast shadow on the ground
quiz.explanation: Core shadow is on the object itself — where no direct or reflected light reaches.

quiz.question: Reflected light is:
options: Light bouncing from nearby surfaces onto the shadow side of an object
quiz.explanation: Even in shadow, surfaces receive some light bounced from the environment.

quiz.question: Chiaroscuro was pioneered by:
options: Caravaggio and Rembrandt — dramatic light/dark contrast
quiz.explanation: These Renaissance/Baroque masters used extreme contrast for theatrical, dramatic effect.

quiz.question: High contrast creates:
quiz.explanation: Strong differences between light and dark are visually exciting and attention-grabbing.

quiz.question: A value scale shows:
options: A range from white to black with gradual grays between
quiz.explanation: Value = lightness or darkness. Training to see values improves all drawing and painting.

lessons.title: Drawing Fundamentals
lessons.content: Drawing is the foundation. Start with gesture drawing (30-60s quick sketches). Use basic shapes for complex subjects. Pencil grades: H = hard/light, B = soft/dark. Shading: hatching, cross-hatching, stippling, blending. Practice contour drawing for hand-eye coordination. Draw daily — even 10 minutes helps.
examples: Gesture: 30-second people sketches capture movement
Cross-hatching: crossing lines create darker areas
Face proportions: eyes at midpoint, nose at 3/4, mouth at 7/8

keyTerms.value study: A drawing focusing only on light and dark, no color
keyTerms.blind contour: Drawing edges without looking at the paper — builds observation skills

quiz.question: Gesture drawing:
quiz.explanation: Rapid capture of essence.

quiz.question: B pencils:
options: Soft and dark — good for shading
quiz.explanation: B = bold/soft.

quiz.question: Improve at drawing:
quiz.explanation: Consistent practice is key.

quiz.question: A value study uses:
options: Only light and dark values — no color — to understand form
quiz.explanation: Working in grayscale forces you to focus on form and light.

quiz.question: Blind contour drawing improves:
options: Observation skills — you learn to really look at your subject
quiz.explanation: By not looking at the paper, you train your eyes to see edges and relationships.

lessons.title: Painting Basics
lessons.content: Watercolor: transparent, mixes on wet paper, hard to correct. Acrylic: versatile, dries fast, layerable. Oil: rich colors, slow drying, blendable. Mix from primaries rather than buying every color. Start with underpainting, then layers: background → midground → foreground. Flat brush for areas, round for details. Clean brushes immediately.
examples: Watercolor: wet paper first, colors flow beautifully
Acrylic: paint sky, let dry, paint trees on top — clean edges
Only NEED red, blue, yellow, white, black — mix everything

keyTerms.impasto: Thick paint application creating visible texture on the surface
keyTerms.wash: A thin, transparent layer of watercolor covering a large area

quiz.question: Fastest drying:
quiz.explanation: Acrylic: minutes. Oil: days/weeks.

quiz.question: Mix everything from:
options: Red, blue, yellow + white and black
quiz.explanation: Primary colors create all others.

quiz.question: Paint background first because:
options: Foreground objects sit on top with clean edges
quiz.explanation: Back to front creates natural depth.

quiz.question: Impasto technique:
options: Thick paint creating visible texture and dimension
quiz.explanation: Van Gogh used impasto — thick swirling paint you can feel.

quiz.question: A wash in watercolor is:
options: A thin, transparent layer covering a large area
quiz.explanation: Washes create backgrounds, skies, and subtle color transitions.

lessons.title: Sculpture and 3D Art
lessons.content: Sculpture techniques: carving (removing material — stone, wood), modeling (adding — clay, wax), casting (liquid into mold — bronze), assembling (joining pieces). Clay is most accessible. Consider all viewing angles — 360°. Relief: raised from background. Freestanding: independent. Modern: installations, kinetic (moving), environmental art.
examples: Michelangelo carved David from marble — removing everything that wasn't David
Clay coil pot: stack and smooth coils
Calder invented mobiles — moving sculptures

keyTerms.relief sculpture: Raised from a flat background, like coins or building decorations

quiz.question: Carving is:
quiz.explanation: Cutting away to reveal form.

quiz.question: Sculpture differs from painting:
quiz.explanation: Depth and 360° viewing.

quiz.question: Easiest beginner material:
quiz.explanation: Affordable and forgiving.

quiz.question: Relief sculpture is:
options: Raised from a flat background — viewable from one side
quiz.explanation: Like coins, building facades, and carved panels — attached to a surface.

quiz.question: Kinetic sculpture:
options: Has moving parts — changes with time or viewer interaction
quiz.explanation: Motion is part of the art — wind, motors, or viewer interaction create movement.

lessons.title: Printmaking
lessons.content: Printmaking creates multiple copies of an artwork from a single matrix (printing surface). Types: relief printing (carve away areas you don't want to print — remaining raised surface gets ink, like a stamp), intaglio (carve lines INTO a surface — ink fills the grooves, surface is wiped clean), lithography (drawing on stone/plate with greasy material — ink sticks to grease, repels water), screen printing (force ink through a stencil on mesh — used for t-shirts and posters), and monoprint (one-of-a-kind print). Linocut is the most accessible: carve a design into linoleum, roll ink on the raised surface, press paper on top. Prints are numbered as editions (e.g., 3/20 means the 3rd print out of 20). Printmaking democratized art: multiple copies meant wider audiences could own artwork, not just the wealthy.
examples: Linocut: carve a flower design into lino → ink the raised surface → press paper → pull a print
Andy Warhol used screen printing to create his famous Marilyn Monroe prints — each slightly different
Japanese woodblock prints (ukiyo-e) influenced Impressionists like Monet and Van Gogh

keyTerms.relief printing: Ink on raised surfaces — carved away areas don't print (linocut, woodcut)
keyTerms.screen printing: Ink pushed through a mesh stencil onto paper or fabric
keyTerms.edition: A set of identical prints from the same matrix, numbered (e.g., 3/20)
keyTerms.matrix: The surface from which prints are made (woodblock, lino, screen, stone)

quiz.question: In relief printing:
options: Raised areas get ink and print — carved areas don't
quiz.explanation: Like a stamp — only the raised surface transfers ink to paper.

quiz.question: Print edition 7/50 means:
options: The 7th print out of a total edition of 50
quiz.explanation: Edition number / total: this is the 7th print from a run of 50 identical prints.

quiz.question: Screen printing is commonly used for:
options: T-shirts and posters — ink pushed through mesh stencils
quiz.explanation: Screen printing applies flat, bold colors — ideal for fabric and poster production.

quiz.question: Printmaking democratized art because:
options: Multiple copies meant more people could own artwork, not just the wealthy
quiz.explanation: Before printmaking, only the wealthy could own original artworks.

quiz.question: The most accessible printmaking technique for beginners is:
options: Linocut — affordable materials, simple tools, immediate results
quiz.explanation: Linoleum, a carving tool, ink, and paper — that's all you need to start.

lessons.title: Mixed Media and Collage
lessons.content: Mixed media combines multiple materials and techniques in one artwork. Collage: cutting and pasting different materials (paper, fabric, photos, found objects) onto a surface — invented by Picasso and Braque during Cubism. Assemblage: 3D collage using found objects. Mixed media can combine: drawing + painting + collage + digital + text. The freedom of mixed media encourages experimentation — there are no rules about what materials can be combined. Found objects gain new meaning when placed in an art context — a rusty key becomes a symbol, a newspaper clipping becomes commentary. Mixed media is ideal for expressing complex ideas because different materials carry different associations. Digital tools (tablets, apps) now extend mixed media possibilities — combining traditional and digital techniques.
examples: Collage: Romare Bearden combined photographs, painted paper, and fabric to depict African American life
Assemblage: Louise Nevelson created wall-sized sculptures from wooden boxes filled with found objects — all painted one color
Mixed media journal: combine drawing, watercolor, magazine clippings, text, and fabric in a personal art journal

keyTerms.collage: Artwork made by gluing different materials onto a surface
keyTerms.mixed media: Art combining multiple materials and techniques
keyTerms.found object: An everyday object repurposed as part of an artwork

lessons.title: Ancient and Classical Art
lessons.content: Cave paintings (Lascaux, 17,000 years ago): first known art. Egyptian: strict rules, important people larger. Greek: idealized human beauty, realistic proportions. Roman: practical — mosaics, architecture, realistic portraits. African: ancient traditions — Nok terracotta, Benin Bronzes. Art served religion, history, and cultural identity.
examples: Lascaux: natural pigments, blown through hollow bones
Greek Parthenon: idealized gods and athletes
Benin Bronzes: among finest metalwork ever

keyTerms.Benin Bronzes: Elaborate bronze from Kingdom of Benin
keyTerms.iconography: The visual symbols and imagery used in artwork to convey meaning

quiz.question: Oldest artworks:
quiz.explanation: Tens of thousands of years old.

quiz.question: Greek art focused on:
quiz.explanation: Perfect proportions.

quiz.question: Benin Bronzes:
options: Sophisticated metalwork from Kingdom of Benin
quiz.explanation: Advanced African artistry.

quiz.question: Egyptian art followed strict rules because:
options: Art served religious and political purposes — consistency was sacred
quiz.explanation: Art was functional — ensuring the dead could live in the afterlife, not for decoration.

quiz.question: Iconography in ancient art:
options: Used symbols to convey meaning — viewers understood the visual language
quiz.explanation: A winged sun in Egypt meant divine protection — symbols carried specific meanings.

lessons.title: Renaissance to Impressionism
lessons.content: Renaissance (1400-1600): perspective, realistic anatomy, oil painting. Masters: Leonardo (Mona Lisa), Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel). Baroque (1600-1750): drama and emotion (Caravaggio). Romanticism (1800s): nature and feeling. Impressionism (1860s-1880s): loose brushstrokes, light effects, outdoor painting (Monet, Renoir, Degas).
examples: Mona Lisa: mysterious smile, sfumato technique
Monet's Water Lilies: same pond, different light
Caravaggio: dramatic chiaroscuro lighting

keyTerms.sfumato: Soft, smoky blending technique pioneered by Leonardo
keyTerms.plein air: Painting outdoors to capture natural light — central to Impressionism

quiz.question: Impressionism:
quiz.explanation: Capturing fleeting moments.

quiz.question: Renaissance introduced:
quiz.explanation: Vanishing points create 3D illusion.

quiz.question: Plein air painting means:
options: Painting outdoors to capture natural light
quiz.explanation: Impressionists left the studio to paint landscapes, cafes, and gardens in natural light.

quiz.question: Sfumato is:
options: A technique of soft, smoky blending between tones — no harsh edges
quiz.explanation: Leonardo perfected sfumato — the Mona Lisa's mysterious expression comes from this technique.

lessons.title: Modern and Contemporary Art
lessons.content: Modern (1880s-1970s) broke all rules. Post-Impressionism (Van Gogh, Cézanne): emotion and structure. Cubism (Picasso): multiple viewpoints. Surrealism (Dalí): dreams. Abstract (Kandinsky, Mondrian): no representation. Pop Art (Warhol): popular culture. Contemporary (1970s-present): installations, performance, video, digital, street art (Banksy).
examples: Guernica: cubist anti-war painting
Warhol's Soup Cans: art vs commercial products
Banksy: humor + political commentary + accessibility

keyTerms.abstract art: No real objects — form and color for their own sake
keyTerms.conceptual art: Art where the idea is more important than the visual result
keyTerms.Pop Art: Movement celebrating popular culture and mass media imagery

quiz.question: Cubism shows:
quiz.explanation: Fragments and reassembles.

quiz.question: Abstract art:
options: No real objects — form and color for expression
quiz.explanation: Communicates through visual elements.

quiz.question: Pop Art celebrated:
quiz.explanation: Elevating everyday objects.

quiz.question: Conceptual art values:
options: The idea behind the art more than the visual object
quiz.explanation: The concept IS the artwork — the physical object is secondary.

quiz.question: Contemporary art includes:
options: Everything: installations, video, performance, digital, and traditional media
quiz.explanation: Contemporary art has no boundaries — any medium or concept is valid.

lessons.title: African Art Traditions
lessons.content: African art is among the oldest and most diverse in the world. It encompasses: sculpture (masks, figures, totems), textiles (Kente cloth from Ghana, Bogolan/mud cloth from Mali), beadwork (Maasai, Zulu), architecture (Great Zimbabwe, mud mosques of Djenné), body art (scarification, paint), music (djembe, mbira, talking drums), and oral traditions (storytelling, proverbs, poetry). African art is rarely created for 'art's sake' — it serves functional, spiritual, and social purposes: masks for ceremonies, figures for ancestor worship, textiles indicating status, and music for healing and celebration. European artists like Picasso, Matisse, and Modigliani were profoundly influenced by African sculpture — its abstract forms and geometric patterns helped inspire Cubism and modern art. Yet African art was long dismissed as 'primitive' by Western museums — this colonial perspective is now being corrected. Repatriation movements demand the return of stolen African artworks from European museums (Benin Bronzes, Ethiopian artifacts).
examples: Kente cloth: each color and pattern has specific meaning — gold = royalty, green = harvest
Nok terracotta sculptures (Nigeria, 500 BCE): among the earliest known African figurative art
Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) was directly inspired by African masks he saw in a Paris museum

keyTerms.mask: Carved face covering used in ceremonies, storytelling, and spiritual practices
keyTerms.Kente cloth: Colorful woven textile from Ghana — patterns carry specific cultural meanings
keyTerms.repatriation: Returning cultural artifacts to their country of origin
keyTerms.functional art: Art that serves a practical or ceremonial purpose, not just decoration

quiz.explanation: African sculpture's abstract, geometric forms helped inspire Cubism and modern art.

quiz.explanation: Labeling complex traditions 'primitive' was a colonial power move — now recognized as wrong.

lessons.title: Art Movements and Their Context
lessons.content: Art movements reflect the society and time that produces them. Realism (1850s): a reaction against Romanticism — painted everyday life honestly, including poverty and labor. Impressionism: rejected studio painting for outdoor observation — coincided with the invention of portable paint tubes and photography. Expressionism: distorted reality to express inner emotions — emerged during WWI's trauma. Dadaism: rejected all artistic conventions — a protest against the madness of war. Abstract Expressionism: post-WWII America — large canvases expressing freedom and individualism (Pollock, Rothko). Each movement was a response to what came before AND to the world around it. Understanding context helps you understand the art. Today's movements reflect our era: digital art, AI-generated art, NFTs, street art, and socially engaged art that addresses climate, inequality, and identity.
examples: Guernica (1937): Picasso's response to the bombing of a Spanish town — art as political protest
Abstract Expressionism emerged as America became a global superpower — art reflecting confidence and freedom
Street art (Banksy, JR): art leaving galleries and entering public space — commenting on society

keyTerms.Expressionism: Distorting reality to convey inner emotions and feelings

lessons.title: Graphic Design
lessons.content: Graphic design communicates visually. Combines typography, images, colors, layout. Principles: hierarchy (important info stands out), contrast, alignment, repetition, whitespace. Serif fonts = traditional. Sans-serif = modern. Tools: Canva (beginner), Illustrator/Photoshop (professional). Good design is invisible — it guides without the viewer noticing.
examples: Poster: bold title, contrasting colors, consistent style
Apple branding: clean, minimal, premium feel
Restaurant menu: elegant font, clear sections

keyTerms.hierarchy: Most important info stands out first
keyTerms.brand identity: The visual system representing a company: logo, colors, fonts, imagery

quiz.explanation: Guide viewer's eye.

quiz.question: Serif fonts:
quiz.explanation: Small strokes on letters.

quiz.question: Whitespace importance:
quiz.explanation: Reduces clutter.

quiz.question: Brand identity includes:
options: Logo, colors, fonts, imagery, and visual style — used consistently
quiz.explanation: Everything visual that represents the brand — consistency builds recognition.

quiz.question: The best design is often:
options: Invisible — it guides without the viewer noticing
quiz.explanation: Good design feels natural — users don't think about it, they just understand.

lessons.title: Photography Basics
lessons.content: Three key settings: aperture (lens opening — controls depth of field), shutter speed (exposure time — controls motion), ISO (sensitivity — controls grain). Composition: Rule of Thirds, leading lines, framing, symmetry. Golden hour provides warm light. Smartphones have made photography universal.
examples: Wide aperture blurs background (portrait mode)
Slow shutter: silky waterfall. Fast: frozen sports action
Leading lines: road disappearing into distance guides the eye

keyTerms.aperture: Lens opening — controls depth of field
keyTerms.depth of field: The range of distance that appears sharp in a photo
keyTerms.ISO: Sensor sensitivity — higher ISO for dark conditions but adds noise/grain

quiz.question: Blur background:
quiz.explanation: Wide aperture = shallow depth of field.

quiz.question: Freeze fast motion:
quiz.explanation: Captures split second.

quiz.question: Golden hour:
options: Warm, soft, flattering light near sunrise/sunset
quiz.explanation: Low-angle light creates warm tones.

quiz.explanation: Shallow DoF = only subject sharp. Deep DoF = everything sharp (landscapes).

lessons.title: Digital Art and Tools
lessons.content: Digital art uses technology as the medium. Tools: graphic tablets (Wacom — draw directly on screen), drawing apps (Procreate for iPad, Krita for PC — free), photo editing (Photoshop, GIMP — free), vector graphics (Illustrator, Inkscape — free), and 3D modeling (Blender — free, industry-standard). Digital advantages: unlimited undo, layers (work on parts independently), infinite color palette, easy sharing and printing. Digital art is NOT 'cheating' — it requires the same artistic skills (composition, color, form) plus technical knowledge. Many professionals use both traditional and digital: sketch on paper, refine digitally. AI art tools (Midjourney, Stable Diffusion) generate images from text prompts — raising questions about authorship, copyright, and the definition of art.
examples: Procreate on iPad: professional illustration with natural brush feel — used by concept artists worldwide
Blender: free 3D software used for animation, game design, and even film visual effects
AI art: type 'sunset over African savanna, oil painting style' → AI generates an image in seconds

keyTerms.layers: Separate transparent sheets in digital art — edit one without affecting others
keyTerms.vector graphics: Art defined by mathematical paths — scales to any size without losing quality

quiz.question: Layers in digital art:
options: Separate transparent sheets — edit one without affecting others
quiz.explanation: Layers are fundamental — sketch on one, ink on another, color on a third.

quiz.question: Vector graphics are special because:
options: They scale to any size without losing quality
They look better at small sizes
quiz.explanation: Vectors use math, not pixels — a logo can go from a business card to a billboard.

quiz.question: The best free 3D modeling software is:
options: Blender — free and used professionally in film and games
quiz.explanation: Blender is industry-standard quality, completely free, with massive community support.

quiz.question: Digital art is NOT cheating because:
options: It requires the same artistic skills plus technical knowledge
It's the same as pressing a button
quiz.explanation: Composition, color theory, anatomy — all still essential. The tool changed, not the skill.

quiz.question: AI art raises questions about:
options: Authorship, copyright, and the definition of art
quiz.explanation: If AI generates an image from a text prompt, who is the artist? These debates are ongoing.

lessons.title: Art in Everyday Life
lessons.content: Art shapes our daily environment. Architecture: form + function. Interior design: comfortable beautiful spaces. Fashion: wearable art. Product design: functional + attractive everyday objects. Urban art: murals and public sculptures make cities vibrant. Art therapy: creative expression improves mental health. Understanding art builds creativity, visual communication, and critical thinking — valuable in every career.
examples: Sydney Opera House: architecture as iconic art
Eames Lounge Chair: comfortable AND beautiful
Hospital murals reduce anxiety, speed recovery

keyTerms.user experience: How people feel when interacting with designed products and spaces

quiz.question: Applied art:
quiz.explanation: Design for daily life.

quiz.question: Art benefits everyday life:
options: Beautiful spaces, functional products, improved wellbeing
quiz.explanation: Shapes environment and health.

quiz.question: Art therapy works by:
options: Using creative expression to improve mental health
quiz.explanation: Creating art reduces stress and processes emotions.

quiz.question: User experience design considers:
options: How people feel when interacting with products and spaces
quiz.explanation: UX puts the user first — how does it feel to open this app, sit in this chair, enter this building?

quiz.question: Studying art helps in non-art careers because:
options: It builds creativity, visual communication, and critical thinking
quiz.explanation: Every field needs creative problem-solving, visual communication, and aesthetic judgment.

lessons.title: Careers in Art and Design
lessons.content: Art careers are diverse and growing. Traditional: fine artist (painter, sculptor), art teacher, museum curator, art restorer, gallery manager. Design: graphic designer, UI/UX designer, product designer, interior designer, fashion designer, architect. Digital: animator, game artist, 3D modeler, visual effects artist, motion graphics designer. Communication: photographer, videographer, social media content creator, brand strategist. Emerging: AR/VR designer, AI art director, UX researcher, design thinking consultant. Building a career: develop strong fundamentals (drawing, color, composition), build a diverse portfolio (your visual resume), specialize as you grow, network with other creatives, and continuously learn new tools and techniques. Freelancing is common in creative fields — offering flexibility but requiring business skills. The creative economy is growing globally — creative industries contribute $2.25 trillion to the global economy.
examples: UI/UX designer: designs app and website interfaces — median salary $80,000+ in many countries
Game artist: creates characters, environments, and animations for video games — massive growth industry
Freelance illustrator: creates artwork for books, magazines, and brands — flexible but must manage your own business

keyTerms.portfolio: A curated collection of your best work — your visual resume
keyTerms.freelancing: Working independently for multiple clients rather than one employer
keyTerms.creative economy: The economic sector based on creativity, ideas, and intellectual property
keyTerms.design thinking: A problem-solving approach using empathy, ideation, prototyping, and testing

quiz.question: A portfolio should:
options: Showcase your best and most diverse work — quality over quantity
quiz.explanation: Curate your strongest pieces — 10 great works beat 100 mediocre ones.

quiz.question: UI/UX design involves:
options: Designing how apps and websites look and feel for users
quiz.explanation: One of the fastest-growing art careers — combining aesthetics with usability.

quiz.question: The creative economy contributes:
quiz.explanation: Creative industries are a massive and growing economic force worldwide.

quiz.question: Freelancing requires:
options: Art skills PLUS business skills (marketing, invoicing, client management)
quiz.explanation: Freelancers are their own business — they need to find clients, set prices, and manage finances.

quiz.question: Design thinking is:
options: A problem-solving approach using empathy, ideation, prototyping, and testing
quiz.explanation: Used by companies like Apple and Google — understand users, brainstorm, prototype, test, refine.
